info.bio:
Harry Lillis "Bing" Crosby (n. 3 de mayo, 1903 - m. 14 de octubre, 1977) fue un cantante y actor estadounidense cuya carrera comenzó en 1926 y terminó con su muerte en 1977.

Fue uno de los primeros artistas multi-media, desde 1934 hasta 1954 Bing Crosby tuvo un casi imbatible éxito de ventas con sus discos, grandes ratings en las radios y películas mundialmente vistas.[1] Es usualmente considerado como uno de los actores musicales más populares de la historia y es actualmente la voz humana más grabada electrónicamente.

scenes.name: Orquestas de baile: Whiteman y Goldkette
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: Músicas «en los intersticios» que las historias del jazz desprecian. Jean Goldkette, más empresario que músico, reúne a Bix, Tram, Venuti, Lang, los Dorsey, Nichols y el arreglista Bill Challis: en 1926 barre a la banda de Fletcher Henderson en un duelo y Rex Stewart la llama «la primera banda blanca de swing». Paul Whiteman, autoproclamado «rey del jazz» (Robert Goffin dedica en 1931 su libro a «Louis Armstrong, el verdadero rey del jazz»), encarga la Rhapsody in Blue a Gershwin, vende millones con «Whispering» y arreglos pseudoclásicos, pero también da cabida a Bix, a los arreglos de Challis («Changes») y a Bing Crosby, que inventa el canto íntimo de la era del micrófono. Para Gioia, la pureza en la música es un mito.

scenes.name: Antecedentes (1892-1950)
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Antes del rock'n'roll: Tin Pan Alley, los primeros discos de blues (Mamie Smith) y de «old-time music», el yodel de Jimmie Rodgers, el crooning de Bing Crosby, el boogie-woogie, el jump blues de Louis Jordan (nacimiento de facto del rhythm'n'blues), la guitarra jazzística de T-Bone Walker, Woody Guthrie como primer gran cantautor y la exótica de Les Baxter. En paralelo, la vanguardia clásica (Russolo, Satie, Varèse, Cage, Schaeffer) anticipa el ruido, el ambient y la electrónica.

scenes.name: 2000: apogeo y caída de la industria
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Los noventa ven el apogeo y la caída de la industria discográfica: el CD multiplica sus ingresos (cinco «majors» controlan el 95% de los discos vendidos en 1999), Mariah Carey bate récords de Presley y los Beatles y «Candle In The Wind» de Elton John supera a «White Christmas» como canción más vendida. Pero en 1999 Shawn Fanning funda Napster y millones de internautas dejan de pagar por la música: en 2001 las ventas caen por primera vez en años.

podcast.title: Transition from Big Band Singer to Solo Star (1942)
podcast.body: Bing Crosby, a former employee singer in a big band, became a major solo radio star due to a loophole in the American Federation of Musicians strike of 1942. As singers were not considered "musicians" by the union, they were exempt from the strike and free to launch independent careers, a new phenomenon at the time. "Bing Crosby had once been a big band employee, but was set free as a result of the musician strike in 1942."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death Prior to Broadcast
podcast.body: Bing Crosby died at age 74 just weeks before the television special featuring his duet with David Bowie, "Peace on Earth / Little Drummer Boy," was broadcast. "poignantly was broadcast just weeks after Bing Crosby died at age 74."

podcast.title: Early Microphone Singer
podcast.body: Bing Crosby is mentioned as one of the performers who benefited from electrical recording, enabling a softer, more romantic singing style facilitated by microphones. He was a prominent "microphone singer" and later a "crooner." "This is where we get performers like Frank Sinatra and Bing Crosby."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Funding of Magnetic Tape Recorder (1940s)
podcast.body: To solve the problem of broadcasting his radio show twice (once for the East Coast and three hours later for the West Coast), Bing Crosby invested $50,000 (over $600,000 in modern money) in Major Jack Mullin's magnetic tape machine. This investment allowed Mullin to perfect the Ampex 200 reel-to-reel tape recorder, which revolutionized radio broadcasting and music recording by enabling editing and time-shifting. "Bing was so interested in the new machine that he dropped $50,000 or more than $600,000 in today's money, so Mullen could perfect his machine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inventor of Pro Celebrity Golf Tournament
podcast.body: The time saved by using the reel-to-reel tape machine for his radio broadcasts, which freed Bing Crosby to pursue golfing, eventually inspired him to create the pro celebrity golf tournament. This made him an early figure in using celebrity status for fundraising. "he was able to invent the pro celebrity golf tournament, turning him into the original fundraising pop singer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Investment in Ampex and Tape Recording
podcast.body: Bing Crosby became an investor in Ampex, an electronic firm that manufactured reel-to-reel machines based on Jack Mullin's German technology. Crosby was motivated by his dislike for having to repeat his national radio show for the West Coast time zone and saw tape recording as a solution to pre-tape his East Coast broadcast. His investment was crucial in developing modern studio techniques. "So Bing became an investor in Ampex, an electronic firm that had been making real-to-real machines based on Moin's German booty."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Investment in Magnetic Tape Technology
podcast.body: Bing Crosby, a notable crooner, invested a significant amount of his own money to bring magnetic tape technology to the commercial market. Magnetic tape was originally a Nazi invention brought back to the Allies as spoils of war. His investment helped revolutionize recording sessions by allowing for editing. "Playing Crosby, one of those awful cruners, invested a lot of his own money in bringing magnetic tape technology to the commercial market."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Microphone's Impact on Vocal Style (Early 20th Century)
podcast.body: Bing Crosby was among the first singers to recognize and exploit the microphone's potential. Prior to its invention, singers needed naturally powerful voices to project over an orchestra. Crosby realized the microphone allowed for a new, "close and personal" singing mood, fundamentally changing vocal performance. "But when the microphone came along, certain singers like Bing Crosby realized that you could use it to create a whole new mood for singing by getting a close and personal."

podcast.title: Pioneer of Magnetic Tape Recording in Radio
podcast.body: Bing Crosby, a major radio star, was instrumental in popularizing magnetic tape recording in the US. Hating to perform two live shows daily for different time zones, his musical director, Merton Mackenzie, introduced him to Jack Mullen's German Magnetophone machines in 1947. Impressed by the sound quality, Crosby invested $50,000 (over half a million today) in Ampex, a recording technology company, and hired Mullen as his chief engineer. This allowed him to pre-record his shows, freeing him to pursue other activities like golfing, and ultimately set the standard for audio and video recording on tape. "This technology meant that he could record his East Coast performance, leave the studio, and then hit the links and let the technicians with their tape machines take care of the West Coast feed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Vocal Style Avoiding Malisma
podcast.body: Bing Crosby is mentioned as a prominent singer from the early 20th century who exemplified the vocal style of hitting notes "dead arm," singing one note per syllable without ornamentation, a widely accepted standard of good singing in that era. "If you listen to any of the great voices of the first part of the 20th century, Sinatra, Bing Crosby, Tony Bennett, they will almost without exception hit the note dead arm, one note per syllable."

concerts.title: Bing Crosby Christmas Special (Late 1977) - Duet Offer
concerts.body: Bing Crosby hosted a Christmas special recorded in London in late 1977 for broadcast in both the US and UK. David Bowie appeared on the special to promote "Heroes," but the TV producers also asked him to sing a holiday duet of "The Little Drummer Boy" with Crosby, which Bowie initially balked at. "In the closing weeks of 1977, Boey appeared on a Bing Crosby Christmas special recorded in London for broadcast in both the US and the UK."

xref.title: Transition from Big Band Singer to Solo Star (1942)
xref.body: Frank Sinatra, like other big band singers, benefited from the loophole in the 1942 American Federation of Musicians strike. Not being categorized as "musicians" by the union, these singers were free to record and embark on solo careers, becoming stars in their own right, independent of band leaders. "And names included Bing Crosby and Frank Sinatra and Perry Como, all former big band singers."

xref.title: Transition from Big Band Singer to Solo Star (1942)
xref.body: Perry Como was one of several big band singers who leveraged a loophole in the 1942 musicians' strike. Since singers were not bound by the union's recording ban, they were able to pursue solo careers, which transformed them into independent stars and personalities. "And names included Bing Crosby and Frank Sinatra and Perry Como, all former big band singers."

xref.title: Early Microphone Singer
xref.body: Frank Sinatra is identified as one of the performers who emerged with the advent of electrical recording and the microphone. This technology allowed singers to adopt a more nuanced style, singing softly and romantically, which led to the term "microphone singers" and later "crooners." "This is where we get performers like Frank Sinatra and Bing Crosby."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Impact on Modern Recording Techniques
xref.body: Along with investor Bing Crosby and guitarist Les Paul, Jack Mullin is credited with giving birth to modern recording studio techniques from the 1950s onward. His work with reel-to-reel tape made it possible for performances to be started, stopped, restarted, and edited with a razor blade and tape. Mistakes could be excised, jokes cut out, and overdubs became possible, allowing parts of a recording to be redone without affecting others. This also enabled the separate control of track volumes and the post-production addition of special effects like reverb and echo, transforming the studio into a musical instrument. "In short, Major Jack Moan, along with his early believer Bing Crosby and guitarist Les Paul, gave birth to modern recording studio techniques."

xref.title: Kurt Cobain's Vaguely Canadian Ancestry
xref.body: Kurt was born on February 20, 1967, at Aberdeen Community Hospital in Aberdeen, Washington. His paternal ancestry traces to a family from Skytown, County Tyrone, Ireland (spelled "Cobane"), who emigrated around 1875 to Cornwall, Ontario, where patriarch Samuel Cobain worked as a shoemaker. Census records confirm a Samuel Cobain, wife, and seven children in Cornwall. They subsequently moved to Gray's Harbor County, Washington, where Aberdeen is located. Kurt's great-uncle Delbert, on his mother's side, was a respected Irish tenor who appears in the 1930 film *King of Jazz* featuring Paul Whiteman and the young Bing Crosby. "Hardly qualifies Kurt as Cancon, but it is still kind of cool."

xref.title: Modern Recording Practices
xref.body: Jack Johnson is used as an example of a contemporary artist who might record music with friends, illustrating how the ability to multitrack, overdub, and edit music on personal devices or in home studios traces back to the magnetic tape technology brought to the US by Jack Mullen and popularized by Bing Crosby. "Same thing if you've ever recorded some music with your buddies, like, say, Jack Johnson."

xref.title: Technical Contributions and Studio Establishment
xref.body: Gabriel was deeply involved in technical advancements, working on the first stereophonic recordings and supervising Bing Crosby's first-ever stereo recording session. She also contributed to establishing RCA's famous Nashville studio and was involved with the label's initial disco releases. "She got very technical, too, working on the first stereophonic recordings."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Unique Musical Style and Thematic Content
xref.body: In 1983, The Smiths distinguished themselves from the dominant heavy hard rock and synthesizer dance music. Their sound was jangly pop with roots in 1950s and 60s music, featuring simple, stark arrangements without big solos or excessive overdubs. Morrissey's vocal style was a croon, likened to Bing Crosby, and his lyrics explored taboo subjects like homosexuality, child molestation, and murder, alongside life and love, but with a unique sense of doomed romanticism and emotional agony. "The Smiths were neither. The music was jangly pop with its roots clearly in the 50s and 60s."
